books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Labor contract, Records of the Field Offices for the State of Mississippi, Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, 1865–1872 (National Archives Microfilm M1907, roll 47)

stimulus.text:
“…the Parties of the second Part are entitled to receive one half of all crops they may cultivate after a full and entire settlement of all claims the Party of the first Part may have against them arising under this Contract… they further agree that said portion of all crops … shall not be used or removed from the Plantation until all their indebtedness to the Party of the first Part is fully and satisfactorily settled.”

—Labor contract, Freedmen’s Bureau records for Mississippi (1865–1872)
stimulus.source_note: Labor contract from the Records of the Field Offices for the State of Mississippi, Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, 1865–1872 (National Archives Microfilm M1907, roll 47), transcribed by the National Museum of African American History and Culture. Public domain (federal record). Ellipses mark omissions inside the passage; “the Party of the first Part” is the landowner and “the Parties of the second Part” are the freed workers.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The sharecropping system spread across the South after the Civil War mainly because

options.text: freedpeople lacked land, and landowners lacked cash for wages.
the federal government ordered all farms to use it.
options.misconception: Background: the government never ordered sharecropping; it grew from bargains between landowners and workers.

options.text: Black families preferred it to owning their own farms.
options.misconception: Background: freedpeople wanted land of their own, “forty acres,” and took sharecropping only because land never came.

options.text: the Supreme Court required it in the Slaughter-House Cases.
options.misconception: Background: the Slaughter-House Cases were about citizenship and butchers, not about farm labor.

rationales.A: Emancipation freed the workers but gave them no land, and the war left landowners with fields but no money. Sharecropping was the bargain both sides fell into: the landowner gave land and supplies, the worker gave labor, and the crop split the difference.
rationales.B: Background: the government never ordered sharecropping; it grew from bargains between landowners and workers.
rationales.C: Background: freedpeople wanted land of their own, “forty acres,” and took sharecropping only because land never came.
rationales.D: Background: the Slaughter-House Cases were about citizenship and butchers, not about farm labor.
rationales.general:
1. Emancipation ended slavery but gave freed families no land to work.
2. The war left landowners with fields and no cash to hire hands.
3. Each side had what the other needed: land on one side, labor on the other.
4. The crop share was the bargain they struck, and it spread because nothing better was offered.
Remember: a system spreads when it solves the problem in front of people, even if it solves it badly.
